text:
Transfer of State Authority to Federal Government. H.R. 4758, Section 4, would provide for Federal regulation of the taking of any endangered animal. Protection from killing or molestation of any endangered animal would be by Federal law. At the present time, Federal authority under the Endangered Species Conservation Act of 1969 does not provide for protection of any endangered animal from killing or molestation. Some species are protected or violators can be prosecuted under certain other Federal statutes—Lacey Act, Migratory Bird Treaty Act, Marine Mammal Act, and Bald Eagle Act, but resident or non-migratory species receive most of any protection they receive through State law.
The <u>Montana</u> Department of Fish and Game says there is no reason for the Federal Government to take over management of resident wildlife under any circumstance. They feel the State can do a much better job of managing and preserving wildlife.
The <u>Texas</u> Parks and Wildlife Department, says there is much of the bill and environmental impact statement they "could endorse but not removal from State jurisdiction of endigenous wildlife forms." They also say "If a State fails to assume the responsibility of managing such forms, within a reasonable period, there might then be a basis for such Federal control."
Prepared comment on the proposed legislation of 1972 (HR 1311) by the Oregon State Game Commission says that existing Federal authority such as the Migratory Bird Treaty Act has not been effective in "enhancing, maintaining, or even protecting wildlife species." As evidence it points out over 65 percent of the species of birds in the 1968 "Red Book" were included in the 1918 Act and in spite of the 1940 Bald Eagle Act, the Southern Bald Eagle is still decreasing.
